Subject: Polaris dedicated – rough GPU footprint ask

Grace / Karthik,

Thanks for the quick intro last week. We're starting to converge on requirements for a dedicated pool for our Polaris v2 LLM and need a rough footprint to include in our internal purchase request (heads-up to procurement shortly). High level: 
- Model: Polaris v2 (1.4T parameters)
- Typical requests: structured conversation + long-context retrieval; average response 300 tokens, peak 1k tokens
- Context window: 64k tokens active; we plan to store fairly large KV cache per session (heavy retrieval patterns)
- QPS: baseline 10 rps, expected peak 35 rps during bursts; latency SLO ~200ms p95 for interactive flows
- Desired quantization options: FP16 (baseline), INT8, and a 4-bit experimental mode — we'd like to understand trade-offs for each on GPU count and per-request latency
- Batch patterns: mostly single-user interactive, occasional 8–16 request batching for backend jobs

Attached a small sample of representative prompts and session lengths (sample_prompts.json). Can you provide an initial slab/tiling approach (if applicable) and a ballpark of how many GPUs we should reserve at commit for each quant mode? Also interested in headroom guidance (10/20/30%).

Procurement timeline: aiming to finalize numbers by mid-July so we can lock a dedicated pool in Q3.

Appreciate any early numbers so we can align finance.

-Mike

Mike —

Thanks, this is very clear and exactly the level of detail we need to start sizing. High-level plan from our side: propose a tiling / slab strategy where the 64k KV cache is sharded across the GPU pool with per-GPU KV segments (slabs) plus a small hot-cache prefix kept on-GPU for low-latency paths. That lets us trade off memory vs. tail latency and gives deterministic paging for very long contexts. Two immediate axes we'll size: (1) model weights footprint + activation workspace, and (2) KV cache per-session slab sizing.

Initial asks from us before the workshop: sample QPS distribution (PDF) would help but your sample_prompts.json is a good start. I'm attaching an initial estimate workbook (polaris-tiling-estimate.xlsx) with a few scenarios: 
- Scenario A: FP16, 64k context, 10 rps baseline, 20% headroom
- Scenario B: INT8, same context, can reduce weight memory ~2x vs FP16 but KV dominates at 64k; lower headroom needs
- Scenario C: 4-bit experimental: big weight savings but added decode overhead; we show CPU/GPU balance notes

Quick note: for interactive SLOs (~200ms p95) we'll recommend reserving a small hot prefix (2–4k tokens) in fast KV memory on each GPU and routing cold-session tokens to slab fetch paths — this keeps p95 tight while preserving overall memory efficiency.

Next step: schedule a 90 minute technical sizing call (I can run the model-memory walkthrough). When's good for your infra/ops and procurement folks this week or next?

Best,
Grace O'Connor

Mike / Grace —

I ran a tight-first-pass set of numbers based on Polaris v2 (1.4T) and the patterns you shared. Put the short version here, attaching the raw calc snippet (kv-footprint-calcs.txt). Full workbook has scenario sheets.

Assumptions: model weights (FP16) ~6.4GB on device after sharding; optimizer/workspace ~1.2GB; per-token KV entry ~64 bytes (key+value pointers + metadata) — at 64k context that's ~4.1GB per session if using full in-GPU KV. We generally expect to shard KV so per-GPU slab holds N sessions * slab_size.

Ballpark per-GPU footprints (single-GPU effective capacity numbers):
- FP16: weights + workspace 7.6GB; hostable KV slab ~10–12GB without offload -> supports ~2–3 heavy sessions (64k) active per GPU at interactive latency targets (with 20% headroom)
- INT8 quantized weights: weight footprint drops to ~3.6GB; workspace ~0.9GB -> frees ~4GB for KV slab; supports ~4–6 heavy sessions per GPU (but decoding CPU overhead increases slightly)
- 4-bit (experimental): weight footprint ~1.9GB; workspace ~0.6GB -> supports ~6–10 heavy sessions per GPU but expect ~10–20% latency penalty on decode path and additional engineering risk for stability under peak burst

Routing and headroom guidance: for your 10 rps baseline / 35 rps peak, assuming mostly interactive single-user traffic and ~200ms p95 target, recommended reserved pool sizes:
- FP16: reserve 16 GPUs (baseline), target commit 20 GPUs (25% headroom) to cover bursty retriever spikes and node-level variability
- INT8: reserve 9 GPUs (baseline), commit 12 GPUs (33% headroom recommended given potential CPU decode contention)
- 4-bit: reserve 6 GPUs (baseline), commit 9 GPUs (50% headroom recommended until we validate tail latency thoroughly)

A few operational notes:
- We recommend a hybrid slab layout: hot prefix (2–4k tokens cached on each GPU) + slab shards for cold KV with prefetching and a tiny async fetcher to minimize p95 impact.
- If you plan heavy batch jobs, plan separate worker pools with larger batch windows and looser SLOs to avoid impacting the interactive pool.
- Canary plan: start with INT8 commit on 25% of traffic for 2 weeks (monitor quality/regression) before moving to larger commit.

I've kept conservative headroom for early phases; we can tighten once we have telemetry from a small canary. Happy to walk these numbers in the sizing call.

—Karthik

Summarizing the thread and next actions so procurement and infra have a single record. Attachments: redwood-tiling-runbook.pdf (operational notes + slab rebalance flow) and the workbook we previously shared.

Summary (TL;DR):
- Recommended commit (initial): INT8 reserved pool = 12 GPUs (covers baseline + 33% headroom for bursts and CPU decode variance)
- Canary: deploy INT8 to 25% traffic for 2 weeks with detailed quality checks and latency telemetry (we'll run auto-regression evals against your prompt set)
- FP16 fallback: keep a small FP16 burst pool of 4 GPUs for high-quality or latency-critical flows during canary
- 4-bit: suggest experimental track only after canary is green; plan for 50% headroom if used in production early

Operational notes (see runbook):
- Slab rebalance: Redwood supports automated rebalancing with session-aware drain. In practice we prefetch slab segments to neighbor GPUs, mark affected sessions as pending, and failover reads to host-offload if necessary. The runbook includes error budgets and escalation playbook.
- Canary and rollout: we will provide a canary dashboard and a rollout policy that supports A/B, canary, and immediate fallback to FP16 variant.
- SLA/commercial: attaching a one-page capacity-commit template and sample monthly range. We'll issue a preliminary quote for INT8 and FP16 options by tomorrow EOD.
